newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher, strong dollar cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher, strong dollar cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened higher on Tuesday, bolstered by a strong dollar.

"The market is opening at new highs because of a tremendous bid on the dollar versus the deutschmark overnight," said Patrick Dimick, trader and Treasury strategist at UBS Securities LLC. The dollar surged to a 23-month high against the mark in London overnight.
The 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond was up 7/32 to 102-2/32 in early trade, its yield at 6.34 percent, versus 6.36 percent at Monday's close.

Dimick said there was "very good buying" of U.S. Treasuries during the London session, led by accounts that bought U.S. 10-year Treasury notes versus the bund, based on the view that the spread between those securities, having widened as much as 45 basis points, will start to narrow.
As to the landscape that the market must explore in New York on Tuesday, the weekly BTM/Schroders and Redbook store sales reports well be very important, said Dimick.

"The key issue is whether the reports will validate the stories of very strong Thanksgiving weekend retail sales that broke yesterday," he said. "Will the weekly reports confirm that picture or confuse it?"

A report on October new home sales, due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, is also an important topic for the market. Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that new home sales occurred at an annualized rate of 772,000 in October, a sharp drop from September's level of 816,000.
"The market expects home sales to come off significantly," said Dimick.

The Conference Board's release of the index of leading economic indicators is expected to be up 0.1 percent for October, after a 0.1 percent rise in September. Due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, this report is not expected to move the market.

But a rumor that the BTM/Schroders weekly retail sales report, due at 0900 EST/1400 GMT, was down 0.2 percent, was said to give the market an extra lift in early trade. A decline in the report would temper the rosy picture of consumer spending engendered by press reports on holiday shopping over the weekend.

Federal funds were trading at a firm 5-7/16 percent in early activity. Analysts at MMS International said settlement of the 14-day cash management bill sold on Monday would keep the pressure on the funds rate. MMS said it expected the Fed to add temporary reserves to the banking system through system repurchases later and that a permanent reserve addition through a coupon pass was also possible.

Dimick said a coupon pass has probably already been priced into the market. "The coupon pass has been a very oversold event," he said. "It's received a lot of attention. We have to see how much the Fed would buy, and how aggressively."
In early trade, the two-year note was up 1/32 to 100-2/32, yielding 5.59 percent.
Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 100-7/32, yielding 5.82 percent. Ten-year notes were up 6/32 to 103-13/32, yielding 6.07 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down three basis points to 4.92 percent. Six-month rates were down two basis points to 5.02 percent. Year bill rates were down one basis point to 5.10 percent.
